name: Tension
summary: Tension is arousal held without release: the viewer knows an event is coming and is made to wait for it. Alternate a wide 50/50 that shows the distance between the parties with matched singles that show intention and inserts that act as the ticking clock (hands, a phone, a weapon, a watch). Make each cycle of shots tighter and shorter, keep the camera still or creeping, and keep the sound sparse. Hold the release until it is almost unbearable, then show it in a shot wide enough to read cause and effect.

color: one warm practical against cool fill
editing: hold the release one beat longer than comfortable
sound: isolated small sounds: a clock, a fingernail, a lighter

rules.then: establish both parties and the space between them in a wide 50/50 before the first single
rules.why: the audience can only fear a distance it has measured; the gap between them is the tension

rules.then: cycle singles and inserts, each cycle one size tighter and shorter than the last
rules.why: shrinking size and shot length raise arousal while information stays constant, so the pressure reads as coming from the scene, not the plot

rules.then: keep the reverse singles matched in size, lens and height
rules.why: matched coverage says neither side has the upper hand, which keeps the outcome uncertain

rules.when: the release (the shot, the answer, the slap)
rules.then: go back to a wider frame for the moment itself
rules.why: a release in close-up hides cause and effect; the wide pays off the geography you built

name: Suspense
summary: Suspense comes from the audience knowing more than the character. Show the threat first and clearly (an insert of the bomb, the figure in the background, the poisoned glass), then cut to the oblivious characters in an ordinary, safely lit room and cross-cut between the two. The room should look normal; the danger lives in the cutting. High angles on the unaware victim make them look small and exposed, and slow pushes toward the hidden threat keep reminding the viewer it is still there.

editing: return to the threat insert more often as time runs out
decide on payoff or defusal and commit

rules.then: show the threat in a clean, readable insert before the characters are introduced
rules.why: suspense needs information; the audience cannot worry about something it has not been shown

rules.then: light and frame them normally, with a slightly high angle
rules.why: the ordinary look sharpens the irony, and the high angle makes them vulnerable without tipping them off

rules.then: return to the threat insert more often and hold each shot of the victims a little longer
rules.why: the contrast between the shortening threat cuts and the leisurely conversation is the engine of suspense

avoid.why: the audience feels cheated; deliver the explosion or the rescue

name: Intimacy
summary: Intimacy is made by removing the world. Medium-long lenses (75-100mm) gently compress faces and throw the background out of focus; dirty over-the-shoulders keep the other person physically present in every frame; matched close-ups make the pair equals. Light soft and warm with a backlight halo, keep the camera still or creeping, let takes run long and lay dialogue across cuts. The audience should feel it has leaned in too.

editing: J-cuts and L-cuts so a line lands on the listener
no cutaways to the room once intimate

rules.then: use dirty over-the-shoulders rather than clean singles so the listener's shoulder or hair stays in frame
rules.why: the foreground body keeps them physically connected in every cut; a clean single would isolate

rules.then: match size, lens and height on the reverses
rules.why: equal framing codes equal vulnerability; mismatching would introduce power

rules.then: move one step tighter (MCU to CU) and slow the cutting, not quicken it
rules.why: proximity rises while time stretches, which is how closeness feels

name: Isolation
summary: Isolation is a frame that is too big for the person in it. Use wide shots with heavy negative space and put the figure small, off-center or short-sided; let the room (empty desks, an unlit kitchen, a window full of other people's lights) say what is missing. Keep the camera still or let it pull away. Cool, desaturated light, long holds, ambient sound and no score keep the audience from offering the character any company. In a crowd, flip it: a long lens isolates one sharp face in a blur of strangers.

color: blue night spill against one warm practical
editing: no reaction shots because no one is there to react
sound: room tone, HVAC hum, distant traffic
a sound from outside that does not include them

rules.then: start wide, with the figure small and off-center in a space built for many people
rules.why: empty chairs and desks state the absence of others without a word

rules.then: keep negative space on the open side and put nothing in it
rules.why: the empty side of the frame is where a companion would be; the eye notices it is vacant

rules.then: pull out slowly or cut to the widest, highest view and hold
rules.why: the pull-out literally removes the audience from the character, leaving them more alone

name: Dread
summary: Dread is anticipation of harm without knowing when or where. Give the viewer space to search (wide lenses, empty backgrounds, doorways), take away information (darkness, backs of heads, foreground occlusion), and slow time (long static holds, imperceptible push-ins, low drones). Delay the payoff; the scare is optional, the waiting is the point.

editing: cut away just before the reveal

rules.when: a character enters an unknown space
rules.then: frame them short-sided with a dark doorway or corridor in the open side of the frame
rules.why: the open side is where the viewer expects the threat; the eye keeps checking it

rules.then: keep it very slow (barely perceptible) and toward the back of the head or an empty space, not the threat
rules.why: slowness implies inevitability; pushing into emptiness makes the audience imagine

rules.then: cut or hold one beat later than comfortable
rules.why: violating expected rhythm is itself unsettling

name: Power Imbalance
summary: Shot/reverse-shot normally codes equality by matching size, lens and height. Power imbalance is made by breaking that match on purpose: the dominant character gets a tighter, lower, closer frame (often a wider lens close in, so they loom), centered or in the foreground, backlit or top-lit; the weaker character gets a looser, higher frame from further back on a longer lens, small, off-center and boxed in by the set. Give the weaker one the reaction shots and the dominant one the last word. When the balance flips, flip the coverage.

color: dark, rich tones around the dominant
flatter, paler light on the weaker
editing: dominant character gets the last word and the last shot
flip the coverage when power shifts

rules.then: shoot the dominant one tighter and from below (chest height looking up) and the weaker one looser and from above
rules.why: mismatched size and height breaks the equality code of matched reverses, so the audience feels the hierarchy before it is stated

rules.then: put a wider lens close on the dominant character and a longer lens far from the weaker one
rules.why: the close wide lens makes the dominant one loom toward camera; the distant long lens shrinks and flattens the other against the wall

rules.then: swap the treatments, ideally inside a single move (a push-in on the newly strong character, or the weak one standing into a low frame)
rules.why: a visible change in coverage tells the audience the hierarchy changed at that exact moment

name: Romance
summary: Romance is a gap that closes. Open with a 50/50 two-shot that shows the space between the two people, cover them in matched singles on long lenses (85-135mm) that flatter faces and dissolve the background, then let the frames and the bodies converge: the two-shot tightens, the camera pushes, and at the peak it orbits so the world spins away behind them. Light warm and backlit (golden hour, candles, practicals with flare), hold shots longer, and give the look between them more time than the dialogue.

editing: give looks more screen time than lines
sound: ambient city or room falling away

rules.when: the pair first sit or stand together
rules.then: establish the gap between them in a 50/50 two-shot
rules.why: romance is the closing of that gap; the audience has to see it to feel it close

rules.then: match the singles in size, lens and height, with at most a slight low angle on the person being fallen for
rules.why: matched coverage codes mutual attraction; a hint of low angle idealizes without creating a power gap

rules.then: move to a tight two-shot and push or orbit slowly
rules.why: the orbit sends the background spinning away so the couple become the only fixed point

name: Comedic Timing
summary: Comedy is causality the audience can read and a beat it can feel. Keep setup and payoff in the same frame (wide or full shots for physical gags, MS two-shots for verbal ones), lock the camera off and frame frontally or symmetrically for deadpan, and light high-key so nothing is hidden. Cut on the beat, never in the middle of a gag; hold one beat on the reaction because the reaction gives the audience permission to laugh. Snap zooms, whip pans and smash cuts are punctuation, used sparingly.

editing: hold one beat on the reaction
never cut inside a physical gag

rules.then: frame wide or full enough that the setup and the payoff happen in one unbroken shot
rules.why: the laugh comes from seeing cause and effect connect; a cut in the middle makes it look faked

rules.then: cut to the reaction and hold it a beat before the next line
rules.why: the reaction tells the audience how to read the moment and leaves room for the laugh

rules.then: lock off, frame frontally and symmetrically, and let performers do nothing
rules.why: a still, formal frame makes absurd content funnier by refusing to acknowledge it

recipes.name: The pratfall with a deadpan witness
recipes.beat: a man confidently carries a tray of drinks across a party and goes down in front of his date

shots.purpose: setup: wide showing his path, the tray, and the hazard on the floor
shots.subject: A
shots.lighting: bright high-key party light
shots.composition: hazard and destination both visible in frame

shots.purpose: insert: the hazard (a spilled ice cube) right in his path
shots.subject: prop

shots.purpose: the fall, in one wide unbroken full shot
shots.subject: A
shots.composition: his whole body and the landing spot in frame

shots.purpose: reaction: B, frontal and still, holds a beat
shots.subject: B
shots.composition: centered, symmetrical

shots.purpose: punctuation: snap zoom onto A on the floor, still holding one unbroken glass
shots.subject: A

recipes.why: The insert plants the hazard so the audience anticipates; the fall plays in one wide so it is real; the still, frontal reaction gives permission to laugh, and the snap zoom lands the topper.

recipes.name: Deadpan two-shot
recipes.beat: two people sit side by side on a couch, one delivers absurd news in a flat voice

shots.purpose: frontal symmetrical two-shot, locked off
shots.subject: both
shots.lighting: flat high-key
shots.composition: perfectly centered, couch square to camera

shots.purpose: frontal single on B absorbing it, no expression change for a beat
shots.subject: B
shots.composition: centered

shots.purpose: back to the identical two-shot for the topper
shots.subject: both

recipes.why: The formal, unchanging frame refuses to react, so the audience does the reacting; returning to the exact same two-shot makes the repetition itself a joke.

avoid.what: cutting in the middle of a physical gag
avoid.why: it breaks causality, and the audience suspects a trick instead of laughing

avoid.what: long lenses and shallow focus on the gag
avoid.why: the setup in the background goes soft and the joke loses its context

avoid.what: low-key lighting
avoid.why: shadow hides faces and props that the joke depends on

name: Awe
summary: Awe is scale contrast plus a witness. Put a tiny human against something vast (EWS, low horizon, massive negative space, often symmetrical) so size is measurable, and pair it with a face looking up in wonder so the audience knows how to feel. Move slowly upward: crane or pedestal up, tilt up, a slow push-in on the face. Backlight, haze and shafts of light give the space volume. Hold the shots long and let the music swell or drop into reverent silence.

editing: face first, then the reveal, then back to the face

rules.then: always include a human figure or known object for scale
rules.why: without a scale reference the brain cannot measure size, and a vast thing reads as merely big

rules.then: show the character's face reacting first, then what they see
rules.why: the reaction primes the audience's emotion and makes the reveal a payoff they have been waiting for

rules.then: move slowly and upward (crane up, tilt up), never fast
rules.why: slow ascending motion reads as reverence; fast motion reads as action and shrinks the scale

recipes.name: The first sight
recipes.beat: a traveler crests a ridge and sees a colossal ancient structure for the first time

shots.purpose: the face: slow push-in as they look up, light changing on their skin
shots.subject: A
shots.lighting: bright backlight wrapping the face, eyes catching the light

shots.purpose: their POV: tilt up the structure, it keeps going
shots.subject: env
shots.lighting: haze and shafts of sun through openings

shots.purpose: scale: crane up and back from behind the tiny figure to the vast structure
shots.subject: A
shots.composition: figure tiny at the bottom center, structure filling the symmetrical frame

shots.purpose: back to the face, held in stillness
shots.subject: A

recipes.why: The face tells the audience how to feel before it sees anything; the tilt makes the structure's height a duration, and the crane from behind the tiny figure gives the scale a measurable reference, then returns us to the human witness.

avoid.what: revealing the vast thing without a human for scale
avoid.why: nothing to measure it against, so it reads as a postcard

avoid.what: quick cutting or handheld during the reveal
avoid.why: awe needs time and stillness to register

avoid.what: flat, frontal midday light
avoid.why: no haze or backlight means no depth or volume in the space

name: Grief
summary: Grief is filmed with restraint. Withhold the face first (from behind, in a doorway, at a distance) so the audience grants the character privacy and leans in; let emptiness stand for the person who is gone (an empty chair, a coat on a hook, half a bed). Use normal-to-long lenses, eye level, still frames or a slow pull-out, soft overcast light and a desaturated palette. Hold long, stay on room tone, and cut late. When news is delivered, stay on the person receiving it, not the person speaking.

editing: stay on the listener when news is delivered

rules.then: frame them from behind or at a distance before any close-up
rules.why: withholding the face grants privacy, and the audience's restraint becomes respect and then empathy

rules.when: news of a death is delivered
rules.then: hold on the person receiving it and let the speaker's words play off-screen
rules.why: the event is the reaction, not the information

rules.then: frame the empty space where the person used to be and hold it
rules.why: emptiness in a familiar place is how loss is actually felt

recipes.name: The empty chair
recipes.beat: after the funeral, a widower sits alone at the kitchen table where his wife used to sit

shots.purpose: from behind in the doorway: his back, the kitchen, her empty chair across from him
shots.subject: A
shots.lighting: soft overcast window light, desaturated
shots.composition: door frame around the scene, empty chair clearly visible

shots.purpose: insert: her reading glasses still folded on the table
shots.subject: prop

shots.purpose: MS profile: he looks at the empty chair
shots.subject: A
shots.composition: him on one third, the empty chair holding the rest of frame

shots.purpose: CU, finally, as he breaks; long lens, from a respectful distance
shots.subject: A

shots.purpose: slow pull-out back through the doorway, leaving him there
shots.subject: A

recipes.why: Starting from behind and through a doorway grants privacy; the glasses and empty chair make the absence concrete; the close-up arrives late and from a distance, so it feels earned rather than intrusive, and the pull-out leaves him alone with it.

recipes.name: The news in the corridor
recipes.beat: a doctor tells a woman in a hospital corridor that her brother did not survive

shots.purpose: wide two-shot down the corridor: the doctor approaching, she stands
shots.subject: both
shots.lighting: flat fluorescent, cool

shots.purpose: stay on her, MCU, as the doctor speaks off-screen
shots.subject: B
shots.composition: doctor's shoulder soft at the frame edge

shots.purpose: back to the wide; she sits down slowly, the doctor waits
shots.subject: both

recipes.why: Holding on the listener makes her face the event; returning to the wide gives her body room to fail and the audience distance to absorb it without melodrama.

avoid.what: pushing into a crying face for the whole scene
avoid.why: it feels exploitative and quickly numbs the audience

avoid.what: swelling score over the first beat
avoid.why: music tells the audience what to feel and replaces the empathy the silence would earn

avoid.what: cutting to the speaker during bad news
avoid.why: the information matters less than how it lands
